This minute body mass reflects the egg diameter of roughly 0.3 millimeters observed in congeneric species, yielding a spherical volume that constrains the initial organic content available to the developing embryo. The swift progression from syngamy to larval release at this temperature underscores the species' strategy of investing in numerous small offspring rather than a few large ones, a pattern common among opportunistic sessile invertebrates that rely on rapid colonisation of ephemeral substrates.

This modest adult body mass places Botrylloides violaceus among the smaller botryllid ascidians, a trait that likely facilitates the high population densities observed on subtidal hard surfaces throughout its introduced range in temperate waters.

Physiological death of the zooid occurs through progressive resorption of the branchial basket and digestive tract, a process that frees space and resources for the next generation of blastogenic buds. This pattern of semelparous zooid reproduction within an iteroparous colony framework is a hallmark of the Botryllinae and represents an efficient strategy for rapid turnover on seasonal substrates.
